newsitem.title: UK: UK wages growth demands tax rises - analysts.
newsitem.headline: UK wages growth demands tax rises - analysts.

text.p: Robust growth in British average earnings, particularly in the service sector, offers a real inflationary threat and would be best dealt with by a rise in direct taxes, economists said on Wednesday.
But that was not going to happen, they added.

Official figures showed annual average earnings growth of five percent in February, up from a revised 4.75 the month before. With a flood of bonus payments paid by the financial service sector in March, that figure could soon rise again.

"There are real warning signals here," said Adam Cole, UK economist at HSBC James Capel. "March, which sees the end of the financial year, is by far the most important month for financial services bonuses. I wouldn't be at all surprised to see another quarter-point rise next month."
The Office for National Statistics said manufacturing pay awards rose by 4.75 percent in the year to February while services wages rose 5.0 percent.

While the difference appears small, Cole said if public sector service pay -- up only about two percent each year -- was stripped out of the equation, private service sector pay looked like it was going through the roof.

The problem with the British economy is that services and retailers are enjoying near-boom conditions but manufacturing continues to lag, weighed by a pound that has rocketed by about 16 percent on a trade-weighted basis since last August.

An interest rate rise could hurt manufacturers even more if it drove the pound still higher but services, which rely much more on bubbling domestic demand, would find tighter monetary policy much less of a constraint.
"The stance of policy is pushing us to a severely skewed economy and a rate rise wouldn't help much," Cole said.
That leaves taxes. But both the ruling Conservatives and opposition Labour Party cannot countenance direct tax increases.

Labour's shadow Chancellor Gordon Brown has pledged to leave income tax rates untouched while Labour leader Tony Blair has promised that value-added-tax will not be extended to areas such as books, transport and children's clothes.
"What we would really like to see is a sharp rise in personal sector taxes but it's not going to happen," Cole said.
John Shepperd, chief economist at Yamaichi International, agreed the service sector, particularly financial services in the City of London, was driving economic growth.

He pointed to London house prices, up about 20 percent on a year before, while in other parts of the country prices have hardly risen at all. Shepperd said basic wages were not rising much in London's square mile. "But bonus payments have been hefty and we're certainly not doing less business in financial services because sterling is strong."
The service sector needs higher interest rates but manufacturing does not, he said. "It's a real dilemma."
Like Cole, Shepperd agreed a fiscal tightening would be ideal. "But it's very unlikely. The Labour Party does not want to be tarred as the party of higher taxes."
Labour is nearly 20 points ahead in most opinion polls. With May 1 elections approaching fast, they are poised to take power for the first time in 18 years.

With Wednesday's economic statistics showing unit wage costs rose by just 2.6 percent in the latest three months, down from 3.1 over the three months to January, productivity is obviously keeping pace with higher wages. Inflation is unlikely to explode.
"If there is an inflation problem in the UK, it is not a massive one. We should not go overboard on this," Shepperd said.
Retail price data, due on Thursday, are likely to emphasise his point. Economists forecast underlying RPI will ease back to 2.8 percent over the year to March, from 2.9 in February.
